title: Expansion Microscopy for Studying Mammalian Neuromuscular Junctions
author: Ramadan, Sheard, et al.

This section explains in detail the NMJ staining protocol that has been used in this protocol.3.Permeabilization and Blocking:a.Following microdissection, transfer the teased muscle fibers to a 24-well plate (Figure 2D).b.Add 4% Triton X (v/v) at RT on a rocker to facilitate antibody penetration (for permeabilization). The volume is variable, where the muscle fibers should be totally immersed in the buffer (in 24 well plates usually 900 μl is enough per well).c.Add the blocking solution containing 4% BSA (w/v) and 2% Triton X (v/v) (Sigma-Aldrich, UK) in RT on rocker (in 24 well plates usually 900 μl is enough per well).4.Antibody Incubation, labeling and Biomolecule Anchoring:a.AChR Labeling: Use Alexa-488 α-Bungarotoxin (α-BTX, Alexa Fluor 488 conjugate, B13422, Invitrogen) to label the AChRs. The applied diluted ratio is (1:500), and the incubation time is 30 minutes at room temperature (20°C–27°C).b.Incubate the muscle bundles overnight (12–20 hours) at 4°C with one of the following primary antibodies:i.Mouse anti-SV2 IgG (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank, University of Iowa) at 1:50 dilution.ii.Mouse anti-NaV1.4 IgG (Anti-NaV1.4 Sodium Channel Antibody-N255/38, Antibodies Incorporated) at 1:500 dilution.Note: Primary antibodies were applied in a blocking solution containing 4% BSA and 2% Triton X.c.After primary antibody incubation, wash the samples four times with 1% PBS, for 20 minutes each.d.Incubate the samples with secondary Antibody: Alexa 594-Goat anti-mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat No: A-11005) was applied at 1:400 dilution (1x PBS) for 5 hours at RT.e.Samples were washed four times with 1% PBS, for 20 minutes each.f.At the end of day 3 (after finishing the staining protocol), wash the labeled muscle fibers two times with 1% PBS (10 minutes each). Then, within the same 24-well plates, add the anchoring regent by applying 0.1 mg/mL of anchoring reagent acryloyl-X (AcX; Sigma-Aldrich, UK) from an AcX stock of 10 mg/ml in (DMSO; Biotium, USA).g.Remove the 24-well plates immediately to dark storage at 4°C overnight (12–20 hours).Note: All of the aforementioned steps are applied in the same 24-well plate (Figure 2D the schematic). Transferring the muscle fibers within the wells by using forceps is safer and easier than trying to suction/add the regents by pipette (to avoid suctioning the fibers mistakenly). Also, the 24-well plate should be always wrapped with aluminum foil to prevent any potential photobleaching of the stained samples.Optional: We recommend the inclusion of a secondary-only control as an optional step, particularly when users introduce novel antibodies or staining combinations. This ensures that any non-specific binding of secondary antibodies is detected without significantly increasing experimental workload.

steps.title: Prepare gel chamber base
steps.instruction: Cover a standard glass microscope slide with a flat, even layer of Parafilm; cut #1.5 (22 × 22 mm) coverslips into rectangular spacers (typically four per coverslip) using a diamond‑tipped glass cutter; attach one spacer at each end of the Parafilm‑covered slide with 2–3 µL dH₂O to improve adhesion.

steps.title: Coat coverslip roof with poly‑L‑lysine
steps.instruction: Place additional #1.5 (22 × 22 mm) coverslips in a clean dish, add 200 µL Poly‑L‑lysine solution (Sigma‑Aldrich, P8920‑100 mL) per coverslip, incubate at room temperature (20 °C–27 °C) for 30 min, rinse gently with sterile dH₂O, and air‑dry completely; these coverslips will serve as the gel‑chamber roof.

steps.title: Assemble imaging chamber
steps.instruction: Fit the poly‑L‑lysine‑coated coverslip onto the Parafilm base using a custom acrylic chamber (square cutout 18 mm or circular cutout 17 mm diameter) and apply PinkySil silicone moulding rubber (SR‑PINKY‑T, Barnes, AU) along the edges; press the acrylic body gently but firmly to ensure uniform adhesion. Ensure all coverslips are clean and dry before assembly.

steps.title: Prepare fluorescent bead PSF calibration
steps.instruction: Vortex 1 µL of 0.1 µm fluorescent bead stock in 999 µL PBS to make a 1:1,000 working dilution; add 5–10 µL of this dilution to 200 µL PBS in an imaging chamber, mix gently, then acquire z‑stack images with a 20× air objective using the same imaging parameters as for expanded samples. Select fields with isolated beads (<10 per field of view) and compute the PSF automatically in Huygens software.

steps.title: Permeabilize and block muscle fibers
steps.instruction: Transfer teased muscle fibers to a 24‑well plate; add enough 4 % Triton X‑100 (v/v) in PBS to fully immerse the fibers (≈900 µL per well) and rock at room temperature; then add blocking solution containing 4 % BSA (w/v) and 2 % Triton X‑100 (v/v) (≈900 µL per well) and continue rocking at room temperature.

steps.title: Label acetylcholine receptors
steps.instruction: Incubate the fibers with Alexa‑488 α‑bungarotoxin (α‑BTX, Invitrogen B13422) diluted 1:500 in the blocking solution for 30 min at room temperature (20 °C–27 °C).

steps.title: Incubate primary antibodies overnight
steps.instruction: Add primary antibody solution (in the same 4 % BSA/2 % Triton X‑100 blocking buffer) and incubate overnight (12–20 h) at 4 °C: either mouse anti‑SV2 IgG (DSHB) at 1:50 dilution or mouse anti‑NaV1.4 IgG (Antibodies Incorporated) at 1:500 dilution.

steps.title: Wash and apply secondary antibody
steps.instruction: Wash samples four times with 1 % PBS for 20 min each; then incubate with Alexa 594‑goat anti‑mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher A‑11005) diluted 1:400 in 1× PBS for 5 h at room temperature; wash again four times with 1 % PBS for 20 min each.

steps.title: Final washes and add anchoring reagent
steps.instruction: At the end of day 3, wash the fibers two times with 1 % PBS for 10 min each, then add anchoring reagent acryloyl‑X (AcX) to a final concentration of 0.1 mg/mL using a 10 mg/mL AcX stock in DMSO; mix gently.

steps.title: Store samples overnight in dark
steps.instruction: Immediately cover the 24‑well plate with aluminum foil to prevent photobleaching and place it at 4 °C in the dark for 12–20 h.

steps.title: Deconvolve acquired images
steps.instruction: Upload the confocal z‑stack images to Huygens software and apply the Classic Maximum Likelihood Estimation (CMLE) deconvolution algorithm, which uses the previously measured PSF.

steps.title: Measure AChR morphology in Fiji
steps.instruction: Load deconvolved z‑stacks into Fiji, create maximum intensity projections, then for each region of interest (ROI) perform: (i) split channels and select the AChR channel; (ii) adjust Threshold (default mode) to match the original image; (iii) Process → Binary → Make Binary; (iv) use the line tool to measure the widest diameter (“Length”) of each AChR strip and record in an Excel sheet as “AChR Strips Width (µm)”; (v) Process → Binary → Skeletonize; (vi) measure the narrowest gap between adjacent strips and record as “Distance between AChR Strips (µm)”; (vii) on the skeletonized image, measure the length of individual AChR stripes and record as “AChR Stripes Length (µm)”. Repeat for additional ROIs.

steps.title: Perform intensity profile analysis
steps.instruction: For each ROI, open the same TIF file, split channels, identify the AChR channel and the second channel (NaV1.4 or SV2), zoom to the ROI, then use Analyze → Plot Profile → Data → Save Data for each channel separately; import the saved data into Excel ensuring equal numbers of data points per channel, then use GraphPad Prism v10 for statistical tests (unpaired t‑test for group comparisons, Pearson correlation for AChR vs. NaV1.4 intensity profiles).

steps.title: Calculate expansion factor and correct sizes
steps.instruction: Determine the expansion factor by dividing the post‑expansion gel dimension by the corresponding pre‑expansion dimension (typically 3.4–4.0×); divide all ImageJ measurements obtained from expanded images by this factor to obtain true physical sizes of structures.

description: Expansion microscopy (ExM) was first introduced over a decade ago.2 Since then, numerous adapted protocols have emerged, facilitating high-resolution imaging of a range of different biological tissues and research samples.3 The concept of super-resolution (SR) ExM imaging is achieved through a specialized sample preparation process, which results in the physical expansion of stained biomolecules.4 Here, we present a detailed protocol for applying the classical 4× ExM protocol to investigate synaptic components of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) in order to reveal its nanoscale morphological features.1 We demonstrate the feasibility of our protocol in thick muscular specimens from both human biopsy samples and mouse tissues, using dorsal interosseous (DIO) muscles from the hand and forepaw respectively. This protocol is relatively straightforward and convenient, taking five subsequent days for completion and requiring only standard laboratory equipment. The workflow is characterized by applying a robust, previously-optimized NMJ immunohistochemical staining protocol on muscle samples5 (with particular emphasis on microdissection) and adopting a classical 4x ExM protocol that was developed to study cardiac ryanodine receptor clusters in cardiomyocytes in vitro,6 but with modifications required in order to make it applicable when working with thick skeletal muscle samples. The protocol also incorporates a simplified method for analyzing NMJ components using the open-source software Fiji. Finally, we highlight key challenges and limitations, along with proposed potential troubleshooting strategies. Our main purpose is to make this protocol widely available to the NMJ research community, as it offers a powerful but practical approach for visualizing NMJ nanostructure in a way that doesn’t require the more extensive resources and technology needed for SR imaging techniques.3 For our initial study1 the decision to use the mouse DIO muscle from the forelimb paw was driven
